Say I have an adjunction F⊣UF⊣UF⊣U, where C⇄FUD\mathcal C \overset U {\underset F \rightleftarrows} \mathcal DCF⇄​U​D. This adjunction is a pair of arrows in the underlying category — most often the category of sets and functions — equipped with proofs of inversion. So long as they are indeed functions, I can apply them to my arrows.

There seems to be no standard notation for any of this stuff. I can name the adjunction — its type is F⊣UF⊣UF⊣U and it is essentially unique, so the type is all that is needed. But there are two functions in it, so the notation (F⊣U)(f)(F⊣U) (f)(F⊣U)(f) would be ambiguous, unless we know the category of fff. In any case, it does not let me refer to either of the functions when I do not yet intend to apply it. If the category of fff is known, the notation (F⊣U)(f)(F⊣U) (f)(F⊣U)(f) seems to be the way to go, but I have never seen it anywhere.

What do I do? Is there a Category Notation Bureau I can request to issue an official notation statement?

If it's for the natural isomorphism Hom(F−,−)≃Hom(−,U−)\text{Hom}(F-, -) \simeq \text{Hom}(-, U-)Hom(F−,−)≃Hom(−,U−), I've seen ♯\sharp♯ and ♭\flat♭ used to denote each arrow, with f♯∈Hom(Fa,b)f^\sharp\in\text{Hom}(Fa, b)f♯∈Hom(Fa,b) and f♭∈Hom(a,Ub)f^\flat \in \text{Hom}(a, Ub)f♭∈Hom(a,Ub) it's transpose. This is the case in Category Theory in Context (Chapter 4) by Emily Riehl.

The problem is that she also uses musical notation for things that do not seem to be meant to be adjunctions, for example in the proof of proposition 2.3.9 on page 64… There is also something called «musical isomorphism» that has the same notation but seems to be specific to differential geometry…
Which version of the book are you looking at? This does not appear in the version on her website.

Oh, it disappeared… My copy is from a while ago, it reads:

Proposition 2.3.9. For any k\mathbb kk-vector spaces VVV and WWW, V⊗kW≅W⊗kVV ⊗_\mathbb k W ≅ W ⊗_\mathbb k VV⊗k​W≅W⊗k​V.

…Found it. It has become 2.3.10 on page 70 and uses a hat now.

For the operation in Luc's answer, some people also use the notation ftf^{\mathsf{t}}ft and call it the tranpose (for both ways). However, it is not clear to me whether that it is what you are asking. Can you clarify the following points?

So long as they are indeed functions, I can apply them to my arrows.

What is "they" here?

But there are two functions in it

What two functions are you talking about? FFF and UUU? If so, then they are named FFF and UUU. (they are functors, not functions)

Ignat Insarov said:

My copy is from a while ago:

Is it a physical copy? I am curious to see what Riehl has to say about musical isomorphisms. (It is the first time I see this terminology.)

A bijection of sets consists of two functions (and two proofs of inversion). In this case, the adjunction at hand furnishes for us a bijection (or, rather, a family of bijections naturally indexed by objects of the categories being adjoined). It is these two functions that I try to refer to. Some people call them adjuncts, but this naming does not seem widely used.

It is an electronic copy but I had it downloaded a while ago. I do not think she refers to it as musical notation anywhere in the book — however, these is an article https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musical_isomorphism that uses sharps and flats. I am going to attach my copy for reference.

Emily Riehl - Category Theory in Context.pdf

I see. Then Luc's and my answer are fine. nlab indeed uses adjuncts, and I agree that I rarely see it. There is no Category Notation Bureau, so you should choose the notation and terminology that you prefer and fits best in your context.

Ignat Insarov said:

I do not think she refers to it as musical notation

Ah ok, I misunderstood your earlier message.

Alright. I have seen this called «transpose» but I am confused why people call it so. It does not seem to have anything to do with transposition of matrices. If we take the free-forgetful adjunction of vector spaces to sets, the adjunct from functions to linear maps performs something I can best describe as multiplication of a matrix by a vector.
Sometimes words mean different things in different contexts. So too in mathematics.

Not when they both concern matrices! This would only confuse everyone! No. I reject this. puffs up

To be serious — there are two possibilities. Either:

  • The person that came up with the term in one context was aware of its use in the other and there is deep wisdom in this pun.
  • There is some other context in which «transposition» makes sense as a name for an adjunct function.

Either would help.

I always thought the correspondence is primarily notational:
D(F(c),d)≅C(c,U(d))\mathbb{D}(F(c), d) \cong \mathbb{C}(c, U(d))D(F(c),d)≅C(c,U(d))

W⟨f(v),w⟩=V⟨v,u(w)⟩W\langle f(v), w\rangle = V\langle v, u(w)\rangleW⟨f(v),w⟩=V⟨v,u(w)⟩

where F:C⇆D:UF: \mathbb{C} \leftrightarrows \mathbb{D}: UF:C⇆D:U is a categorical adjunction, and f:V⇆W:uf : V \leftrightarrows W : uf:V⇆W:u are adjoint linear maps.

Ignat Insarov said:

the adjunct from functions to linear maps performs something I can best describe as multiplication of a matrix by a vector

Can you explain your intuition here? What matrix and what vector are being multiplied?

Here is my intuition. Given a set SSS and a space VVV, the adjunct of a function f:S→U(V)f: S \to U(V)f:S→U(V) is the linear map obtained by linearly extending fff to the vector space spanned by SSS (i.e. the free vector space F(S)F(S)F(S)). The adjunct of a linear map T:F(S)→VT: F(S) \to VT:F(S)→V is the restriction of TTT to SSS.

There is only, so far - an entirely formal analogy between category theory and linear algebra/calculus that coend calculus notation exploits.

In this analogy, set valued functors are like real valued functions/vectors, homs are like the inner product, and therefore the yoneda lemma is like solving for a coefficient of an orthogonal basis, because representable functors are like the dirac delta function.

The adjoint and transpose terminology matches the terminology from linear algebra relative to this apparently formal analogy.

I asked a question about it here:

https://categorytheory.zulipchat.com/#narrow/channel/229199-learning.3A-questions/topic/Linear.20Algebra.20.3D.20Category.20Theory/with/566409324

@Ralph Sarkis  I do not know if I can explain my intuition but it would be my pleasure to try.

Let me denote arrow sets with the arrow notation, as customary in type theory. For example c→Cc′c →_\mathcal C c'c→C​c′ would be the set of all arrows in C\mathcal CC with source ccc and target c′c'c′. I am also going to provisionally call the function ∀cd.(F(d)→Cc)→(d→DG(c))∀ c d. (F (d) →_\mathcal C c) → (d →_\mathcal D G (c))∀cd.(F(d)→C​c)→(d→D​G(c)) that implements an adjunction F⊣GF ⊣ GF⊣G between categories C\mathcal CC and D\mathcal DD the FFF-GGG adjunct, and its inverse the GGG-FFF adjunct. I am also going to call the value of an adjunct at fff the adjunct image of fff.

Now let me wield this notation to explain my proposition that in the free-forgetful adjunction F⊣UF ⊣ UF⊣U the UUU-FFF adjunct implements multiplication of a matrix by a vector. The lollipop x⊸yx ⊸ yx⊸y will get a cameo appearance as the set of all linear maps from xxx to yyy, like in literature on linear logic.

  1. Let us have a function of type S→U(V)S → U (V)S→U(V). We can ask for its UUU-FFF adjunct image, which would be of type F(S)⊸VF (S) ⊸ VF(S)⊸V. But we are going to forget that the adjunct image is a linear map — with UUU as an intermediary we can treat it like a function. This UUU-modified UUU-FFF adjunct would have type (S→U(V))→(F(S)→V)(S → U (V)) → (F (S) → V)(S→U(V))→(F(S)→V).

  2. But S→U(V)S → U (V)S→U(V) is in one to one correspondence with the type of matrices with columns indexed by SSS — let us call it XXX. If we apply the (F(S)→_)(F (S) → \_)(F(S)→_)-(_×F(S))(\_ × F (S))(_×F(S)) adjunct (it comes from the Cartesian closed structure of functions between sets), we get X×F(S)→VX × F (S) → VX×F(S)→V.

  3. This X×F(S)→VX × F (S) → VX×F(S)→V type we now read as something that takes a matrix and a vector and computes a vector. May as well call it «multiplication». It does seem to be doing what one would expect from multiplication of a matrix by a vector.

In short, we apply an adjunct to the adjunct.

Ignat Insarov said:

Alright. I have seen this called «transpose» but I am confused why people call it so. It does not seem to have anything to do with transposition of matrices. If we take the free-forgetful adjunction of vector spaces to sets, the adjunct from functions to linear maps performs something I can best describe as multiplication of a matrix by a vector.

Adjunctions take their name from linear algebra, where two operators are adjoint when ⟨u,Tv⟩=⟨Su,v⟩\langle u, Tv \rangle = \langle Su, v \rangle⟨u,Tv⟩=⟨Su,v⟩. In particular for finite dimensional vector spaces, if T=A⋅−T= A \cdot -T=A⋅− is multiplication by a matrix, then S=AT⋅−S = A^T \cdot -S=AT⋅−. Hence the transpose.
This is true for a real inner product; for a complex inner product we take the conjugate transpose. (I mention this just in case any analysts or physicists are lurking around.)
